title: Miriam believed (Sotah 12a–13a)
hookLine: young Miriam urges her parents not to give up, foreseeing the deliverer
tomorrow: Pharaoh's daughter saves the baby. why does she get a Hebrew name?

cards: A kitchen table, late, and the news is bad. The grown-ups are talking low. Then somebody says it: maybe we should just stop trying.

In the Talmud's telling of the start of Exodus, the bad news is Pharaoh's decree against the Hebrew newborn boys, told here without detail. The one who gives up is Amram, the leading man of his generation.
And the one who won't is his young daughter. Her name is Miriam.

teach.b: Amram reasons: if the sons will be taken, why have children at all? So he separates from his wife, Jocheved, and the Talmud says the other men followed him. Then Miriam speaks up.
Father, your decree is harsher than Pharaoh's. Pharaoh's is against the boys. Yours is against the boys and the girls.
Amram listens. He remarries Jocheved, and the others do too. Miriam goes further: she says her mother will have a son who will save Israel.
When Moses is born, the Talmud says, the whole house fills with light, and her father kisses her head.
Then the baby has to be hidden in a basket on the Nile, and her father taps her head and asks: so, where's your prophecy now?
That, the rabbis say, is why the Torah tells us: "And his sister stood afar off, to know what would be done to him."
The Torah doesn't name her there; the rabbis hear Miriam, watching her own hope float down the river, and staying.
One to tell a friend tonight: in this midrash, a child's argument changes a grown man's mind, and the result is Moses. Miriam never says it will be easy. She just won't let fear make the decision.

how: At some seders today, Miriam is remembered alongside Moses and Aaron, and some families set a cup of water for her on the table, recalling the midrash of Miriam's well.

s: in the midrash, Miriam promised everything would go smoothly
she foresaw a deliverer, then watched him hidden on the Nile. she stayed anyway.
Miriam's argument is with her father, not with Pharaoh
she tells Amram his decree is harsher than Pharaoh's.
the Torah names Miriam in the basket scene
it says his sister; the rabbis hear Miriam there.

games.q: your best friend was turned down by a summer program and says she won't apply anywhere next year either. by Miriam's argument, what do you point out?
o: not applying is a bigger no than the rejection ever was.
she's right: protecting herself from more hurt is the wise move.
the next place will surely say yes, so there's nothing to fear.
games.why: Miriam told Amram his decree was harsher than Pharaoh's: giving up shut more doors than the threat did. she promised no easy ending.

practice: Choose someone close to giving up on something: an application, a recovery, a hard year. Write them a short message that doesn't promise how it ends, only that you're still watching with them, the way Miriam stood by the river.
Send it, or keep it ready to send when the sit ends.

wordCard.voice: Miriam believed: the Talmud's young Miriam, who argued her father out of despair and stood by the river to see her hope through.

orig.note: Hebrew name: Miriam, sister of Moses and Aaron.

carryVoice: Your line: miriam believed. Hope that stays by the river, even when it floats away. Thirty-seven of forty.
